A betrayal of the right to health

By: Johann Botha | Production

Proposal


Show:

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Despite a transformed and well funded public healthcare system, its benefits to the poor remains questionable

Summary:
Its been 20 yrs since the traditional health care system of SA was overhauled. This transformation was greeted with specific reform measures addressing inequity, disempowerment, underdevelopment and inconsistent service delivery. But despite our extensive and well-funded public health care system, on which our government spends 12% of the national budget and 4% of GDP - our public healthcare sector is consistently rated below average by international health care monitor groups.


In the past fifteen years the industry has been dominated by the irony of health workforce redundancy and vacancy freezes, shortages of medical staff, graduate unemployment and cuts in education and training provision. Arguably, recent trends have shown a slight reverse in this downward spiral, but overall, in this time frame - health outcomes have worsened.

Our case study for this insert clearly highlights the shortcomings of the public health system (despite its proclaimed intension to ensure that every South African, irrespective of race, gender, geographic location and socio- economic status) and how it still fails those who so desperately rely on it in their most vulnerable state: the uneducated and the poor.

After being referred from Nelmapius Clinic, then to Mamelodi Hospital and onwards to Steve Biko, the mother of a 2 year old toddler spends two months sitting next to her sick child's bed whilst never fully understanding whats happening to her baby. After being ignored by doctors & ill-treated by nurses she left with a partially paralysed child. We look at the back-bone of the PHC, the human resource component and what actually happens inside a public health care facility.

Press Release:


Hospital Neglect
A mother spends three days in the waiting area of a public hospital with a desperately ill toddler, while - at another academic hospital - nurses are caught sleeping while babies lie unattended. Why are the country’s most vulnerable still deprived of adequate healthcare? Carte Blanche uncovers severe negligence at two Gauteng public hospitals.


Script:


Video Audio
External shots of RDP houses in Nelmapius township, internal shots of pictures against the wall, showing simplicity and poverty "Girl singing gospel song
Tessa crying out that she is the mother, and she needs to know whats wrong with her child"
Link Devi outside Tessa's house Tessa is a single mom living here in Nell Mapius, east of Pretoria.. A year ago her 3 year old daugther Tashnee contracted a rare and destructive disease -TB Menangitis.
This is the most dangerous of all types of TB. Even Teshnee’s vaccination was not enough to safeguard her.
The earlier TB meningitis is diagnosed and treated, the better the baby's chances of a full recovery. But in the early stages it is difficult to distinguish from other infectious diseases, and if you miss this small window of opportunity, the end result could be severe brain damage, paralysis, or even death.
When Teshne got sick, her mom took time off from work and they went to the first level of public health available to them – the local clinic. Unfortunately Teshne was not examined by a doctor and only saw a nurse.
Tessa "Toe se hulle vir my nee dis tonsillitis. Hulle het toe vir my dinges gegee, antibiotics en panado stroop. Dis toe reg, gekyk hoe lank werk die antibiotics, maar Teshnee het net erger geword.
Then they told me that it was tonsilitis. They gave me antibiotics and panado syrup. I waited to see when the antibiotics would work, but Teshne's condition only worsened"
In an area where both TB and meningitis are prevalent, the nurse should have told Tessa to bring the child back if there was no improvement in 48 hours. This she did not do, and when Tessa returned 10 days later with a very ill Teshne, this window of opportunity was already closing. But all was not lost yet.
Tessa " Die susters het toe rondgeval, hulle weet nie wat gaan aan nie. Hulle het toe ander dokter toe geroep. Die dokter het
haar kom kyk, haar nekkie gevoel en toe se sy vir my nee, dit is moontlik meningitis.
The nurses ran around, not knowing what was going on. They called a doctor. The doctor looked at her, felt her neck and told me that it was possibly meningitis"
Realising the urgency, the doctor put her on a drip and sent mother and child by ambulance to the next level of the public health system – Mamelodi hospital.
Link Around 42 million South Africans rely on our public health system – that's 84% of our population.
V/O The 410 public hospitals across the country provide more than 85 000 beds. According to 2016 figures tell us that there are 18 600 doctors and about 68 000 nurses.
V/o Because time is of the essence, meningitis is considered an emergency and the note from the clinic doctor meant that Teshnee should have been helped immediately. But, Tessa was told to wait. Worried about losing her place in the queue she didn’t go home.
Tessa "Ons het da gesit op ’n bankie, nie ’n comfortable stoel of iets nie, op ‘n bankie gesit, en wag vir ‘n bed, want daar was nie beddens nie.
We sat there on a bench, not even a comfortable chair, on a bench, and waited for a bed, because there were no beds available"
Tessa noticed that Teshnee's clothes were wet, the drip was leaking.
Tessa "Ek gaan toe na die een van die susters toe ek se vir haar die drip lek, sy se dis nie haar werk nie
I went to one of the nurses and told her the drip was leaking. She said it wasn't her job."
Later another nurse removed the drip. Tessa says no one examined her child or gave her any medication. Valuable hours were being lost in this race against time. They waited the entire day and whole night, without receiving food, water or even a blanket for the sick child.
Tessa "Gelukkig het ek ‘n stukkie koek van haar verjaarsdag gehad, en toe is dit in die sak, toe maak ek dat sy daai stukkie koek eet, die volgende dag toe bring my ma-hulle vir my kos en water
Fortunately I had a piece of her birthdaycake in the bag, so I made her eat that. The next day my mother brought us food and water"
On Day Two, they continued waiting on the bench. A doctor passing by stopped to have a quick look.
Tessa " en hy lees toe die brief wat hulle ons gegee het by die kliniek. En hy se toe nee sy het nie Meningitis nie, hy los toe die saak net daar. Hy het haar nie eers ondersoek nie, of haar nekkie gevoel soos die dokter by die kliniek dit gedoen het nie.
And he read the note they gave us at the clinic. And he said no, it's not meningitis, and left it at that. He did not examine her, or even felt her neck as the doctor at the clinic had done."
Eventually Mother and child spent a second night on the bench, while little Teshne’s condition was rapidly deteriorating. By Day Three she had still not been admitted, examined or given any medication.
Tessa "Op die 3de dag, die aand. Toe kry ons eerste ’n bed.
On the third day, in the evening, we got a bed"
Tessa was told to go home and return the next morning to wash and feed her child. Despite being on unpaid leave, she was back early the next morning –
Tessa "Kom in die saal in, daars my kind, besig om ’n fit te kry. Ek kom daarso, ogies rol om, ek weet nie wat gaan aan nie want dis die eerste keer wat ek sien sy kry ’n fit, eerste keer wat ek sien hoe ’n fit lyk.
I came into the ward and there was my child, having a seizure. Her eyes were rolling, I did not know what was happening as it was the first time I saw her having a fit, the first time I saw what a fit looked like"
Unbeknown to her, seizures are a sign that the window of opportunity was closing fast. The doctors now did the tests that should have been done when the child arrived 4 days earlier.
Despite our requests, the provincial health department simply refused to make anyone to comment about Tessa's experience at Mamelodi Hospital.
Link So once again mother and daughter were put on an ambulance and sent to the next tier in the healthcare system and in this case it was Steve Biko Academic Hospital.
Prof Green heads the paediatric unit and is proud that in spite of challenges, critically ill children are dealt with straight away.
Prof green We never show anyone away, we make a plan.
He is also adamant that from here on, Teshne received the correct treatment.
Prof Green: Director of Paeds & Child Health the day she came into the hospital we knew she had meningitis, she was having seizures or fits and those were appropriately managed
" But, by now the window of opportunity had all but closed.
3 weeks after she was admitted, the build-up of fluid in her brain had to be drained and surgeons operated to insert an external shunt."
Neurosurgeon Its putting a tube into the right ventricles where fluid accumulates so that this fluid can be released.
It seems that communication with the frightened mother was not effective.
Tessa "Hulle kom kyk vir haar, elke dag, maar niemand se vir my wat makeer sy nie. Die enetjie praat met daai enetjie, ek sit daar, niemand sien vir my as die mammie om te se - jou kind makeer nou dit, ons gaan nou die doen om die beste te doen vir Tashnee nie laat sy kan gesond raak of so nie. En dit gaan nou al toe vir ’n maand wat ons daar is.
They came to look at her daily, but no one told me what was wrong with her. This one is talking to that one, i'm sitting there, nobody sees me as the mother and tells me this is what is wrong with your child, we are now going to do this, to try our best to get teshne healthyvagain. And this has now already been a month that we were there."
Tessa relied on what the nurses told her and on what she overheard when doctors did their rounds.
The shunt carries its own risks, if it gets blocked, the excess fluid cannot drain and the damage is exacerbated.
Neuro Blockage, it means there's something in the tube, like, you know, a clot. So you can either suck it open or put a new shunt
According to Tessa this is exactly what happened …..
Tessa "Die pyp het uitgehang ne, en sy vat toe water van daai pyp af, hulle moes nou gaan kyk is dit bacterial of is dit viral in tessie se water, kom ons se breinwater. Maar die tweede keer wat sy trek, trek sy so hard dat daar bloed uitkom en sy los dit net so, en die ding blok toe
The pipe was hanging out, and she drained water from the pipe, they had to go and see if it was bacterial or viral, in her let us say brainwater. But the second time she pulled so hard that blood came out, and then she left it just like that, and it blocked."
Neuro There was no incidence of blockage that we identified during the care of this child.
Tessa "Die nurste het gebel. Die dokter het gebel, dat hulle moet afkom, hulle moet die ding kom fix, want daar waar tessie le in 8.6 is nie die regte plek nie want hulle werk nie met die external shunts nie. Hulle werk nie met kinders met shunts nie. Agt dae gaan verby. Niemand van hulle kom om die ding te kom unblock nie.
The nurses phoned. The doctor phoned that they had to come down, to fix this thing. Because, where tessie was, in 8.6, it wasn't the right place to be because they don't work with external shunts. 8 days went by. Nobody came to unblock this thing"
Neuro That doesn't seem accurate as I say. Every day we do a round and see all our patients. Starting in the ICU, through to casualty, through to the wards
Tessa "Nou se nou vir my, in daai agt dae, wat as teshne nou moes weggegaan het? Want daai ding het geblok.
Now tell me, in those 8 days, what if Teshne passed on? Because that thing was blocked"
She says that at no point did anyone inform her that her child would never be the same again.
Tessa I had to see it for myself that she was paralysed
Prof green Yes, we are guilty sometimes of talking about patients and around patients without explaining it to parents and for that I apologise, we really don’t want that level of service what reflects our department
V/O Apart from non-caring attitudes, tessa says she was also the victim of racism. In one incident, she pointed out that Teshnee's bed was soiled, and was told to change it herself. At the linen cupboard, another nurse accosted her
Tessa "Die een suster se vir my: ja julle coloureds dink julle kan hier kom en kom oorvat, ek is like, ek wil net linen he vir my kind, laat sy kan le want sy het seer
the one nurse said to me, yes, you coloureds think you can come here and just take over. Im like, I just want linen for my child, so she can lie down, she is hurting"
Anna Mowayo is the Head of Nursing
Anna we dont take racial issues very lightly, we’ve got some senior staff which are on suspension because of racial issues
We found an insider who confirmed Tessa’s allegations of non-caring nursing staff. Our source also took our camera in.
"Footage / V/O
Alarms going off next to the bed of a paralysed child whilst everyone is in the kitchen " Nurses on shift are divided into teams to stagger their breaks, and ensure there are always enough nurses in the ward.
Anna They are also delegated to go for their first or second or third tea or lunch
Here the nurses are all in the tea room. Our camera shows there is no one around. Yet, for the last 45 minutes the alarm had been ringing, indicating that this paralysed 10 year old with severe brain damage was in need of help…
Anna It was like seeing red infront of my eyes. But we have already put up some systems
Our source says this happens all the time, and that there is an even bigger problem. Many nurses seem to come on night shift with the intention to sleep...
Anon Source They come here to sleep
Our footage, taken over months, confirms that these are not talking about isolated incidents - sleeping nurses, deserted wards, nurses having social gatherings in the kitchens and backdated patient charts.
According to our source, because they are sleeping, they often don't administer the required patient care. On this patient's chart nothing was filled in after midnight. Then suddenly, at shift change, the chart is complete, as if everything was done on time during the night.


"Teshne stayed in hospital for almost two months. When she was sent home, she was paralysed on the one side, had lost her speech and now has to be fed through a tube.

TB Meningitis is a terrible disease."
Medically her case is considered a success, because she survived
Dr green Our mortality is around 10%, so 90% of children coming into my paeds ICU at the extremists of life survive my facility. Those are internationally competitive statistics

"Three months later, there is some improvement. But the experts say she will never make a full recovery. Tessa is struggling to hang on to her job and provide the high level of care Teshne now needs.
As always her mother and friends are supporting and helping her.

Such is the life of the poor, who happen to be the vast majority of our population. "

Ek kom daarso, ogies rol om, ek weet nie wat gaan aan nie want dis die eerste keer wat ek sien sy kry ’n fit, eerste keer wat ek sien hoe ’n fit lyk. I came into the ward and there was my child, having a seizure. Her eyes were rolling, I did not know what was happening as it was the first time I saw her having a fit, the first time I saw what a fit looked like" Unbeknown to her, seizures are a sign that the window of opportunity was closing fast. The doctors now did the tests that should have been done when the child arrived 4 days earlier. Despite our requests, the provincial health department simply refused to make anyone to comment about Tessa's experience at Mamelodi Hospital. Link So once again mother and daughter were put on an ambulance and sent to the next tier in the healthcare system and in this case it was Steve Biko Academic Hospital. Prof Green heads the paediatric unit and is proud that in spite of challenges, critically ill children are dealt with straight away. Prof green We never show anyone away, we make a plan. He is also adamant that from here on, Teshne received the correct treatment. Prof Green: Director of Paeds & Child Health the day she came into the hospital we knew she had meningitis, she was having seizures or fits and those were appropriately managed " But, by now the window of opportunity had all but closed. 3 weeks after she was admitted, the build-up of fluid in her brain had to be drained and surgeons operated to insert an external shunt." Neurosurgeon Its putting a tube into the right ventricles where fluid accumulates so that this fluid can be released. It seems that communication with the frightened mother was not effective. Tessa "Hulle kom kyk vir haar, elke dag, maar niemand se vir my wat makeer sy nie. Die enetjie praat met daai enetjie, ek sit daar, niemand sien vir my as die mammie om te se - jou kind makeer nou dit, ons gaan nou die doen om die beste te doen vir Tashnee nie laat sy kan gesond raak of so nie. En dit gaan nou al toe vir ’n maand wat ons daar is. They came to look at her daily, but no one told me what was wrong with her. This one is talking to that one, i'm sitting there, nobody sees me as the mother and tells me this is what is wrong with your child, we are now going to do this, to try our best to get teshne healthyvagain. And this has now already been a month that we were there." Tessa relied on what the nurses told her and on what she overheard when doctors did their rounds. The shunt carries its own risks, if it gets blocked, the excess fluid cannot drain and the damage is exacerbated. Neuro Blockage, it means there's something in the tube, like, you know, a clot. So you can either suck it open or put a new shunt According to Tessa this is exactly what happened ….. Tessa "Die pyp het uitgehang ne, en sy vat toe water van daai pyp af, hulle moes nou gaan kyk is dit bacterial of is dit viral in tessie se water, kom ons se breinwater. Maar die tweede keer wat sy trek, trek sy so hard dat daar bloed uitkom en sy los dit net so, en die ding blok toe The pipe was hanging out, and she drained water from the pipe, they had to go and see if it was bacterial or viral, in her let us say brainwater. But the second time she pulled so hard that blood came out, and then she left it just like that, and it blocked." Neuro There was no incidence of blockage that we identified during the care of this child. Tessa "Die nurste het gebel. Die dokter het gebel, dat hulle moet afkom, hulle moet die ding kom fix, want daar waar tessie le in 8.6 is nie die regte plek nie want hulle werk nie met die external shunts nie. Hulle werk nie met kinders met shunts nie. Agt dae gaan verby. Niemand van hulle kom om die ding te kom unblock nie. The nurses phoned. The doctor phoned that they had to come down, to fix this thing. Because, where tessie was, in 8.6, it wasn't the right place to be because they don't work with external shunts. 8 days went by. Nobody came to unblock this thing" Neuro That doesn't seem accurate as I say. Every day we do a round and see all our patients. Starting in the ICU, through to casualty, through to the wards Tessa "Nou se nou vir my, in daai agt dae, wat as teshne nou moes weggegaan het? Want daai ding het geblok. Now tell me, in those 8 days, what if Teshne passed on? Because that thing was blocked" She says that at no point did anyone inform her that her child would never be the same again. Tessa I had to see it for myself that she was paralysed Prof green Yes, we are guilty sometimes of talking about patients and around patients without explaining it to parents and for that I apologise, we really don’t want that level of service what reflects our department V/O Apart from non-caring attitudes, tessa says she was also the victim of racism. In one incident, she pointed out that Teshnee's bed was soiled, and was told to change it herself. At the linen cupboard, another nurse accosted her Tessa "Die een suster se vir my: ja julle coloureds dink julle kan hier kom en kom oorvat, ek is like, ek wil net linen he vir my kind, laat sy kan le want sy het seer the one nurse said to me, yes, you coloureds think you can come here and just take over. Im like, I just want linen for my child, so she can lie down, she is hurting" Anna Mowayo is the Head of Nursing Anna we dont take racial issues very lightly, we’ve got some senior staff which are on suspension because of racial issues We found an insider who confirmed Tessa’s allegations of non-caring nursing staff. Our source also took our camera in. "Footage / V/O Alarms going off next to the bed of a paralysed child whilst everyone is in the kitchen " Nurses on shift are divided into teams to stagger their breaks, and ensure there are always enough nurses in the ward. Anna They are also delegated to go for their first or second or third tea or lunch Here the nurses are all in the tea room. Our camera shows there is no one around. Yet, for the last 45 minutes the alarm had been ringing, indicating that this paralysed 10 year old with severe brain damage was in need of help… Anna It was like seeing red infront of my eyes. But we have already put up some systems Our source says this happens all the time, and that there is an even bigger problem. Many nurses seem to come on night shift with the intention to sleep... Anon Source They come here to sleep Our footage, taken over months, confirms that these are not talking about isolated incidents - sleeping nurses, deserted wards, nurses having social gatherings in the kitchens and backdated patient charts. According to our source, because they are sleeping, they often don't administer the required patient care. On this patient's chart nothing was filled in after midnight. Then suddenly, at shift change, the chart is complete, as if everything was done on time during the night. "Teshne stayed in hospital for almost two months. When she was sent home, she was paralysed on the one side, had lost her speech and now has to be fed through a tube. TB Meningitis is a terrible disease." Medically her case is considered a success, because she survived Dr green Our mortality is around 10%, so 90% of children coming into my paeds ICU at the extremists of life survive my facility. Those are internationally competitive statistics "Three months later, there is some improvement. But the experts say she will never make a full recovery. Tessa is struggling to hang on to her job and provide the high level of care Teshne now needs. As always her mother and friends are supporting and helping her. Such is the life of the poor, who happen to be the vast majority of our population. "

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): Despite a transformed and well funded public healthcare system, its benefits to the poor remains questionable
metadata.Summary: Its been 20 yrs since the traditional health care system of SA was overhauled. This transformation was greeted with specific reform measures addressing inequity, disempowerment, underdevelopment and inconsistent service delivery. But despite our extensive and well-funded public health care system, on which our government spends 12% of the national budget and 4% of GDP - our public healthcare sector is consistently rated below average by international health care monitor groups. In the past fifteen years the industry has been dominated by the irony of health workforce redundancy and vacancy freezes, shortages of medical staff, graduate unemployment and cuts in education and training provision. Arguably, recent trends have shown a slight reverse in this downward spiral, but overall, in this time frame - health outcomes have worsened. Our case study for this insert clearly highlights the shortcomings of the public health system (despite its proclaimed intension to ensure that every South African, irrespective of race, gender, geographic location and socio- economic status) and how it still fails those who so desperately rely on it in their most vulnerable state: the uneducated and the poor. After being referred from Nelmapius Clinic, then to Mamelodi Hospital and onwards to Steve Biko, the mother of a 2 year old toddler spends two months sitting next to her sick child's bed whilst never fully understanding whats happening to her baby. After being ignored by doctors & ill-treated by nurses she left with a partially paralysed child. We look at the back-bone of the PHC, the human resource component and what actually happens inside a public health care facility.
